    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the entire basketball world has spent the past five months or so trying to figure out what exactly caused the beef, or, well, lamb chops and gravy, between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown.
    • According to recent reports, we know the Celtics tried to trade Brown for Giannis Antetokounmpo.
    • In a recent development, regardless, there are clearly some hard feelings here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the entire basketball world has spent the past five months or so trying to figure out what exactly caused the beef, or, well, lamb chops and gravy, between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown. The two coexisted harmoniously as teammates on the Boston Celtics for the better part of a decade. They won a championship together and reached the Eastern Conference Finals five times. That run ended this summer with Boston's stunning decision to swap Brown for Paul George and draft picks, and we've never quite gotten to the bottom of what's happened since.

    According to recent reports, we know the Celtics tried to trade Brown for Giannis Antetokounmpo. After moving Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers, Brad Stevens spoke about the team's need to both spread its financial resources and its usage among a wider group of players. Celtics broadcaster Brian Scalabrine claimed that Brown went to the organization with a list of demands that, if not met, would be followed by a trade request. Brown's camp has denied this claim, and Scalabrine himself has walked it back. Marc Spears reported in July that he had heard Brown felt like the Celtics treated Tatum as though he was the organizational favorite.

    In a recent development, regardless, there are clearly some hard feelings here. Brown claimed last offseason that the 2025-26 season was his personal favorite as a professional. Tatum missed most of that season, and Brown had his best statistical season. Brown claimed early this season that Tatum has a "hell of a PR team," and then he snubbed him at tip-off before their first game as opponents, a Celtics victory. That game was owned by George, Brown's replacement in Boston.

    Sources indicate that so far, the partnership has been harmonious. George is outplaying Brown thus far this season. He's been among the NBA's very best 3-point shooters, has spearheaded a system shift in Boston's defense that has finally allowed the Celtics to generate some turnovers, and he's done so on fewer shot attempts per game (15.7) than Brown has taken in any season since the 2019-20 campaign. Boston's vision for the George fit has proven accurate, and that's been as true in the press as it has been on the court.

    George addressed his partnership with Tatum in an interview with The Athletic on Wednesday, and he made it clear that his role is to "help JT," in clear deference to Boston's remaining superstar. "I'm just not one of those guys that have to have an ego," George said. "My ego comes from what I do on the court when the ball gets thrown up and how I impact the game and how I affect the game in all aspects. My ego doesn't have to come from me stroking it or me thinking I'm bigger than someone or better than someone.

    "But with that is, I know where I'm at in my career. I'm at the end of my career. Tatum, JT has (many) more years ahead of him, and he's someone that I admired from afar. And to see where he's taken his game, how much better he's gotten and him having all the tools and weapons to be the best player in the league, how can I help that? How can I support that and get him there?".

    George and Brown are fundamentally different players. Brown, younger and a better scorer off the dribble, was well-suited to lifting last year's Celtics to a surprising 56-win season despite their shorthanded roster. But George's superior shooting and low-maintenance playing style have suited Tatum perfectly, and the fact that he's at a point in his career in which he's eager to take a backseat to Tatum helps with whatever palace intrigue occurred between Tatum and Brown at the end of their joint run.

    Recent findings suggest that if Brown was indeed frustrated with the idea of playing second fiddle to Tatum, it hasn't shown in Philadelphia. His 76ers are 12-3, he's openly called them Tyrese Maxey's team, and he played a key role in recruiting LeBron James, another ball-dominant star, to join the team in free agency. His usage on this star-studded 76ers roster is at its lowest rate since the 2019-20 season. Clearly, this was not as simple as Brown wanting his own team as so many suggested.

    But something created a rift in Boston that led to where we are now, and so far, everyone involved should be happy with how this has played out. The 76ers and Celtics have the two best records in the Eastern Conference. George is playing better in Boston than he ever did in Philadelphia. Tatum is playing better with George than he ever did with Brown. And Brown has become an essential component of a different contender rather than being forced to start from scratch on a bad team as he would have if he'd been traded to the Milwaukee Bucks for Antetokounmpo.

    On the court, at least, egos haven't been a problem for anybody, and the deal is working out for everyone.

    Woeful Man Utd have no excuses, Carrick is under substantial pressure

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that this was a kick in the midriff for Manchester United.
    • They profited from the first one with Phil Foden sent off after hitting out at Bruno Fernandes – in retaliation – after he was booted in the backside by the United captain who somehow went unpunished.
    • But then City played three quarters of this 199th Manchester derby with just 10 men and came out on top with the inevitable and outstanding Erling Haaland scoring his ninth goal against United to become the top scorer in Premier League meetings between these rivals.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that this was a kick in the midriff for Manchester United. Not once. But twice. And, then, most painfully, a third time with a dismal, dispiriting defeat.

    They profited from the first one with Phil Foden sent off after hitting out at Bruno Fernandes – in retaliation – after he was booted in the backside by the United captain who somehow went unpunished.

    But then City played three quarters of this 199th Manchester derby with just 10 men and came out on top with the inevitable and outstanding Erling Haaland scoring his ninth goal against United to become the top scorer in Premier League meetings between these rivals. And that was a far more painful and damaging blow.

    Erling Haaland has put Manchester City ahead in the derby after a VAR check ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/V0DCwryhFy.

    On a day in which thousands of fans protested, accusing co-owners Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers – with Avram Glazer joining Ratcliffe in attendance – of treating them like “s---”, United unfortunately left a nasty whiff of being just that out on the pitch.

    United were frankly, woeful. They lacked belief and imagination and attacking instinct and too many of their players – their apparent major players – went missing when they needed to stand up and take the game by the scruff of the neck. They could not break down City’s defence and failed to be a front-foot team who can dominate the ball. Which is surely what they aspire to be?

    According to recent reports, they hit the post twice – through Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo – with efforts from 25 yards. And those two local lads were by far their best players. Without them, United carried so little threat, were so blunt, that it was shocking.

    Sources indicate that the question for Michael Carrick, the Manchester United head coach, is simple: what is he trying to do with this team? Can they only ever depend on counter-attacks?

    It has been revealed that afterwards Haaland talked about City’s “personality, character” and that was exactly what United lacked. They did not adapt a tactical plan to combat 10-man City’s desire to keep their wingers high and wide, and break with intent and still try and attack.

    Sources indicate that it was telling that so little did City’s upcoming head coach Enzo Maresca worry about United that he did not add a defensive player, and when he took off Rayan Cherki at half-time, he replaced him with the equally creative Iliman Ndiaye who impressed. Maresca knew United needed space to run in behind and denied them that. It was that simple.

    City also struck the post with United goalkeeper Senne Lammens tipping an Enzo Fernández shot against the frame of the goal, and the visitors were worthy winners as they preserved their perfect start to the season to draw level on points with leaders, Arsenal.

    City handled the occasion and the – admittedly toothless – opposition superbly under their fresh head coach and will clearly be Arsenal’s closest challengers this season.

    According to recent reports, maresca delivered a masterclass. For Carrick? This was a disasterclass. An object lesson in how not to use a man-advantage. And now United will have to endure even more City songs after being outplayed at home like this.

    Was it complacency? Was it inability? Was it a damning lack of courage, confidence, belief even? On the pitch and in the dugout United were far too passive. This was not how a big team plays and Carrick needs to wake up.

    In a recent development, the former midfielder did so well last season to guide United into Champions League qualification but so far this campaign he has given the impression that his job is done. Rather than that the real work starts now.

    There was controversy around the red card and the goal. There is no doubt Foden had to go. But what about Fernandes? He clearly kicked Foden as he was on the ground with the midfielder reacting instinctively, two-footing him in the gut.

    It meant he became the first City player to be dismissed in a Manchester derby in the league since Bernardo Corradi in December 2006 and will be punished with a three-match ban for violent conduct.

    To make matters worse for Foden, who missed out on the World Cup, it happened in front of Thomas Tuchel who names his England squad for the Nations League campaign on Friday.

    My sense is that while United fans generally understand and agree with the decision to stick with Carrick, they hope he is the long-term answer to get the club back to winning the Premier League or Champions League, while the rest of the world doubts it.

    To most, it feels like Carrick remains an interim solution in all but name, entrusted with the keys to Old Trafford until a super coach can move in during the summer of 2027. Carrick will not see it that way, of course, but there are certain perceptions which will be tough to shake off.

    Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the season’s first Manchester derby, with midfield rebuilds the theme of the summer on both sides of town.

    Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi could all be involved for City, who lost Rodri and Bernardo Silva in the engine room, while United have recruited Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos in an attempt to address a long-standing problem.

    Sources indicate that rodri’s departure and a Community Shield shellacking by Arsenal prompted some gloomy forecasts for Enzo Maresca and City, but confidence has grown since. The late turnaround at home to Bournemouth on the opening weekend could well look very vital in a few months’ time, while Crystal Palace and Coventry have also been put away. Victory in Porto was probably Maresca’s most impressive result to date at City, though winning at Old Trafford would usurp that. Three points for City would mean they join Arsenal on a maximum of 12 points from four games.

    It has been a patchy start to the campaign for United and Michael Carrick, and this afternoon’s result will go a long way to shaping perceptions of where they are. The concession of a late equalise at Everton, in addition to a dreadful loss at Hull, adds a degree of pressure. United will be buoyed by their performance in this fixture in January, when they delivered possibly the best performance of the post-Ferguson years to slay City in a 2-0 win that could well have been four or five.

    With Tielemans, Bruno Fernandes and Kobbie Mainoo prominent in midfield, United are trying to shift to a more possession-heavy approach, but any success against City in recent times has tended to come on the counter-attack. Maresca’s team have had lots of the ball in their first few games of the season, so that is the expected pattern again.Full team news on the way later.

    Industry News: Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

    📅 20 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • According to recent reports, rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22.
    • It has been revealed that manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    According to recent reports, rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

    It has been revealed that manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

    Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

    According to recent reports, however, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

    United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

    Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

    The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

    Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

    Sources indicate that on the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

    Industry observers note that around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

    Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

    Industry observers note that additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

    In a recent development, after the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

    From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

    According to recent reports, in possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

    Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:.

    Sources indicate that despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

    Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

    Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

    Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

    United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

    According to recent reports, even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

    As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

    Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

    Recent findings suggest that hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla called on star forward Jayson Tatum to be "better" after he was called for a controversial technical foul in the closing seconds of Wednesday's 105-101 loss, which effectively sealed the game for the Denver Nuggets.

    It has been revealed that "We can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret it a certain type of way," Mazzulla said after the game. "Gotta be better.".

    Industry observers note that with 6.4 seconds remaining, Jamal Murray worked off a huge screen from Nikola Jokić, created space with a nasty step-back on Neemias Queta and buried a difficult jumper to give the Nuggets a three-point lead. The Celtics, who had led by as many as 17 late in the first half, still had a chance to tie, however. At least, they did, until Tatum threw the ball toward referee John Goble.

    The baseline official, Eric Dalen, immediately hit Tatum with a technical foul. Murray stepped to the line and made the free throw to put the Nuggets up by four.

    Recent findings suggest that "I told [Dalen], like, I wasn't mad. Wasn't a foul on me; we just called a timeout," Tatum stated. "John Goble called a timeout and pointed at our bench. Thought he was looking this way, but yeah, he called a tech. For me, just find the female ref that was there, or the other ref, and whoever was probably closest, I should have just gave them the ball.".

    Jamal Murray hits a clutch jumper to extend the Nuggets the lead to 3, with 6.4 seconds remaining in regulation.The Celtics call a timeout, and Jayson Tatum throws the ball towards the ref John Goble, who wasn't looking, and receives a technical foul, which Murray converts to… pic.twitter.com/PZtzl0zs3D.

    Tatum's controversial technical capped a brutal second half for the Celtics and their star.

    After scoring 20 points in the first half to help the Celtics build a 17-point lead, Tatum managed just four points in the second half on 2-of-6 shooting with five turnovers. Notably, he missed mid-range attempts on back-to-back possessions in the final two minutes. The first could have pushed the Celtics' lead back up to three, while the latter would have put them in front.

    It has been revealed that "The four turnovers I had in the third quarter really put us out of sync," Tatum said. "In those situations, I gotta communicate better, I gotta execute better, I gotta take care of the ball. I think that kinda put us in a hole, and was the turning point for the game.".

    This defeat was the first time all season that the Celtics have lost back-to-back games. Now 11-4, the Celtics are 1 ½ games back of the Philadelphia 76ers for the No. 1 seed in the Eastern Conference. Come April, when seeding battles are heating up, the Celtics may rue this one.

    In a recent development, in the second half, as their lead melted away, the Celtics turned the ball over 11 times, were called for 20 fouls (which led to 22 Nuggets free throws) and shot 2 of 19 from 3-point range. Two of the Celtics' four defeats this season have now involved a major blown lead: 22 points against the Detroit Pistons on opening day and 17 points against the Nuggets.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Vanessa Bryant, the widow of Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant, has denied a report that she is teaming up with two-time Lakers champion Pau Gasol to attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Sparks.
    • "Another rumor out today… I have never had any conversations about being an NBA or WNBA owner.
    • Sports Business Journal reported on Wednesday that Bryant and Gasol were interested in the Sparks, which were put up for sale in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Vanessa Bryant, the widow of Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant, has denied a report that she is teaming up with two-time Lakers champion Pau Gasol to attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Sparks.

    "Another rumor out today… I have never had any conversations about being an NBA or WNBA owner. If that was true I would announce it. I'm just over here undecided on what seasonal coffee flavor I like and over caffeinated," Bryant wrote on Instagram. "I can only speak for myself. I don't know what anyone else does or does not have going on.".

    Sports Business Journal reported on Wednesday that Bryant and Gasol were interested in the Sparks, which were put up for sale in October. Owner Mark Walter, who has been shedding assets amid an FBI and SEC investigation into his wealth management firm, is seeking a record-shattering $700 million for the franchise and its yet-unopened practice facility, according to Bloomberg. The current record for a WNBA team sale is $300 million, which Tilman Fertitta paid for the Connecticut Sun before moving the franchise to Houston to revive the Comets.

    Notably, Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, who purchased the Lakers from Walter earlier this year, are reportedly uninterested in the Sparks. Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer reportedly considered bidding on the team in 2024, but is right now prohibited for submitting a bid because he is serving a one-year suspension from the NBA over his role in the Aspiration scandal. However, at least one of the groups bidding for the Sparks, a group of investors put together by Swish Partners, would consider moving the team to Ballmer's Intuit Dome.

    In a recent development, gasol already has a financial stake in the WNBA, as he invested in the league's 2022 capital raise. Bryant frequently attends Sparks games and has brought WNBA players in to host clinics at the Mamba & Mambacita Sports Foundation. The late Kobe Bryant was a prominent figure in the women's basketball community, especially coaching his late daughter Gianna's AAU team. Gianna hoped to play for the University of Connecticut and presumably the WNBA afterward before tragically dying in the helicopter accident that killed her father and seven others in 2020.

    Recent findings suggest that several former NBA players own or have owned minority stakes in WNBA teams, including Magic Johnson (Sparks), Dwyane Wade (Chicago Sky), Kyle Lowry (Toronto Tempo) and Grant Hill and Chris Webber (the upcoming Detroit expansion team set to begin play in 2029). However, no former NBA player holds the governorship of a WNBA team. Gasol could change that. If we expand to immediate family, Bryant could become the first spouse of a former NBA player to hold a controlling interest in a WNBA team, though at this stage, the exact structure of a possible Bryant-Gasol bid and the other investors who could be involved are not clear.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well. Though the final score demonstrated only a seven-point margin, the Miami Heat led by 26 after three quarters and were never in much danger. The defeat dropped the Bucks to 1-14 on the season. The greatest player in their franchise's history now wears another jersey, and they're at the beginning of what figures to be a very long rebuild. Things are bleak.

    According to recent reports, the question here is how bleak. Milwaukee knew it would spend this season in the cellar. It probably expects to live there for a few years. But how far away from winning seriously are the Bucks really? Are they further from genuine contention than any other team in the NBA? Who, right now, has the bleakest long-term outlook?

    To be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity. We don't care if you have a chance to be a plucky .500 team. No, the barometer we're using here is how likely each team is to reach a conference finals in the next five seasons. We're accounting not only for players on the existing roster, but long-term financial flexibility, available draft assets and the competence of the front office helming these organizations. With all of that in mind, let's rank the NBA's most hopeless long-term outlooks.

    The broad sentiment following their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard was that the Clippers faced the bleakest future in the entire NBA. That's probably overstating things slightly.

    Remember, we're talking about a Los Angeles team here. Someone, inevitably, is going to want to play for them. All it takes is one player bucking the league-wide trend against superstar free agency and they're back in business. They have an owner who will spare no expense in pursuit of wins, and there's a 26-year-old All-Star in Darius Garland already on the roster. Couple that with the hope generated by No. 5 overall pick Keaton Wagler, and while the path here is extremely narrow, it exists. If the Brooklyn Nets could build a contender without draft picks in the late 2010s, it's theoretically possible for the Clippers to do the same.

    Of course, the Nets weren't subject to that league-wide pivot away from free agency. They didn't have to trade picks to get Kevin Durant or Kyrie Irving in the door. It's much, much harder nowadays to import talent like that without sacrificing picks that the Clippers frankly don't have. The five first-round picks they were docked in the Leonard investigation left them fully Stepien-locked: while they will have (not especially valuable) first-round picks in odd-numbered years moving forward, they can't trade any of them yet.

    There's also the reputational hit the Clippers just took. Will players interested in winning want to risk their careers on a team that cheated? Can the Clippers even appeal to such players given their asset deficit? These are going to be real hurdles. Their path to the conference finals might rely on a star who's not especially competitive. After all, anyone serious about winning could find a team closer to doing so.

    Recent findings suggest that they're a blank slate with one very promising prospect. Darius Acuff is putting up star box-score numbers in his rookie season. That's by no means a guarantee of future stardom, of course. He's as inefficient as you'd expect a rookie to be on this volume. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey or Dwyane Wade ever did over a full season. But Acuff has a path to becoming one of the NBA's best offensive point guards. These aren't totally empty calories.

    Industry observers note that there's nothing else here. No other notable prospects aside from a handful of likely long-term bench youngsters (Dylan Cardwell, Maxime Raynaud, Emanuel Sharp). Sacramento mostly controls its own picks (aside from the 2031 swap it inexplicably gave San Antonio in the DeMar DeRozan sign-and-trade), but that means less than it used to in the lottery reform era. Its books slowly clean up in the offseasons to come, with Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter expiring after this season and Domantas Sabonis and Malik Monk joining them in the summer of 2028, but Sacramento's forays into cap space have typically been unsuccessful. This isn't exactly a desirable destination. That's what happens when you miss the playoffs 19 times in 20 years.

    That's what separates Sacramento from fellow "one possible star, otherwise blank slate" candidates like the Chicago Bulls. With the hire of Bryson Graham to run basketball operations, the Bulls at least appear to be trending towards becoming a normal organization. Normalcy has eternally eluded Sacramento. The burden of proof is on the Kings. When you've been a mess for 20 years, it's on you to prove that you've cleaned up your act. We'll trust the Kings when they've earned it and not a second sooner.

    For now, they can at least start by actually keeping their success stories in the building. They've kept only one first-round pick this decade through the end of his rookie contract: Keegan Murray, who is now pretty substantially overpaid. Meanwhile, Tyrese Haliburton has blossomed into a superstar in Indiana, while their entire 2021 draft class (Davion Mitchell and Neemias Queta) now starts for Eastern Conference championship hopefuls. They had the unanimous Coach of the Year and the Executive of the Year and fired both within two years. The Kings can't help themselves.

    It has been revealed that there's far more talent in the cupboard here than in Sacramento, but the same organizational concerns apply. The Joe Dumars regime makes mistakes -- the two-year minimum for DeAndre Jordan, not waiting until after the 2025 Finals to trade Indiana its 2026 pick back, everything Shamit Dua has reported about the infamous Derik Queen trade -- that typical teams would never dream of.

    There is not a discernible strategy here besides, seemingly, "acquire players who can put the ball through the hoop." There are a lot of decent individual creators on this roster. None of them synergize well because so few of them can consistently make 3s and all of them are on-ball players with stylistic clashes. The Pelicans have seemingly made the determination, for instance, that Queen cannot play significant minutes alongside Zion Williamson. That's a reasonable choice... but then why is Williamson still on the team? Or, if the Pelicans view him as a fixture, why make such a risky trade for Queen in the first place?

    The trickle-down effect of putting all of these dribblers on the same team is that none of them seem happy to be on it. Dejounte Murray asked for a trade. Jordan Poole is making googly eyes at the Warriors. Trey Murphy has reportedly signaled a desire to move. What is the plan here? What kind of team are the Pelicans trying to build? What do they view as their path to genuine winning?

    Sources indicate that that's what distinguishes Upcoming Orleans from Sacramento. If the Kings get a few more high draft picks and use them on players that complement Acuff, I'd see the vision. It would require Acuff becoming an All-NBA scorer and those picks hitting, but I see the sort of teams they could build, even if they're unlikely to actually do so. I have no earthly idea what the Pelicans would do with a few high picks because talent is not currently the problem. It's how they're using and nurturing it. It's just hard to envision a team with so little understanding of how to balance skill sets and bring out the best in their players making a serious playoff push. Something significant in the organization would have to change.

    They're the best team on this list in the present, and they've clawed their way back to .500 after a miserable start that included leaks about the team's lack of a point guard. Again, we're dealing in upside here. That's what the Suns lack.

    It has been revealed that they control none of their own first-round picks in the seven-year tradable window except for their 2032 selection... which is frozen because they spent the 2024-25 season above the second apron. Even if they had picks, the Suns under Matt Ishbia have never displayed any discipline in using them. Ishbia traded nearly a full draft for Kevin Durant mere days after acquiring the team, spent an unprotected 2031 pick on three far lesser choices that amounted to Mark Williams and a Jusuf Nurkić cap dump, and then spent their 2033 pick as soon as they could access it to get Miles Bridges, whom they've been meaningfully better without thus far this season.

    The most talented players here are all right around their physical peaks. Devin Booker is 30. Dillon Brooks turns 31 this season, and Bridges turns 29. They're going to get worse, not better, and without draft picks, their means of replacing them are minimal. Even the diamonds they've dug out of the rough are on the older side. Collin Gillespie is 27. Jordan Goodwin is 28. The truly young players, like Khaman Maluach and Rasheer Fleming, have thus far underwhelmed. The younger, star-level talent here is Jalen Green, who plays Booker's position and has been a disaster on both ends this season. Why exactly is he still starting over Gillespie? Are the Suns just trying to salvage his trade value?

    Recent findings suggest that teams like the Clippers, Kings and Pelicans are at least young enough and financially flexible enough to grow. The Suns, at least from an asset and financial standpoint, are essentially all-in on a Play-In-caliber roster. That Play-In-caliber roster is going to get worse as it gets older and more expensive and, without access to top talent in the draft, replenishing it is going to be borderline impossible.

    According to recent reports, the Bucks cherry-pick traits from all of our other selections. The Clippers circumvented the cap; the Bucks are getting investigated for doing so with Gary Trent Jr. The Pelicans have a roster full of overlapping skill sets; the Bucks have a million shooting guards, which made the decision to re-sign Trent for $64 million all the stranger. The Suns don't control any of their own picks and the Bucks won't until 2031 at the earliest. The Kings have the NBA's least-successful owner in Vivek Ranadivé, while the Bucks may have the NFL's in Jimmy Haslam, though he technically won't become governor until 2028 due to Milwaukee's bizarre ownership structure (another point against them, as successful teams tend to have stable leadership rather than rotating five-year terms).

    According to recent reports, who is going to be the best player on the team in five years? Brayden Burries is the best long-term prospect, but he profiles as more of a high-end role player. Tyler Herro was an All-Star in the sense that Norman Powell and D'Angelo Russell were All-Stars: they put up substantial numbers in a weak Eastern Conference. Kel'El Ware was the lottery ticket from the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade and he's been so bad that he's somehow playing less than he did on a Heat team that was trying to win. Without access to their own picks or a market that tends to draw free agents, they're basically hoping someone internal (Nate Ament? Ryan Rollins?) breaks out or that they hit on a pick far later than you should rely on.

    You could argue that just by virtue of being in the Eastern Conference, the Bucks have a cleaner path to the final four than those West teams do because they don't have to worry about Victor Wembanyama or the specter of healthier versions of the Oklahoma City Thunder down the line. That's fair, but as we've seen this year, injuries loom over every season. You know what else the West has aside from those two juggernauts? The four other teams on this list. The Bucks, by a wide margin, are the most hopeless team in their own conference. They're starting from the absolute bottom.

    Industry observers note that this was potentially avoidable. Had they acted sooner and traded Antetokounmpo in 2025 when the whole world knew a deal was eventually coming, they could have secured a stronger return and set themselves up for a quicker turnaround. Alas, the Bucks chose to waive-and-stretch Damian Lillard, locking them into $22.5 million in dead money through the end of the decade so they could sign Myles Turner to a contract that is increasingly looking like $28 million or so per year in... close to dead money. Milwaukee got its championship in 2021, but at this rate, it's going to be a while before it sniffs another one.

    #176245. Breaking: Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Problems

    📖 Baca

    Breaking: Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Problems

    📅 25 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • Sources indicate that tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short.
    • Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Sources indicate that tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX).

    Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

    On the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

    Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 Pressing System.

    In a recent development, the Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

    According to recent reports, A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

    The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim indicated some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The issue, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

    Tottenham’s Width-Based Strategy.

    Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

    The half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

    Hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

    Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

    Sources indicate that in general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, showed excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He quickly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

    Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses.

    A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

    In a recent development, due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too promptly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

    Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

    An additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant issues in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

    2-0 and 50% Possession at Halftime.

    Recent findings suggest that by the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate newly introduced build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

    In a recent development, additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

    Despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham revealed general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

    Through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

    In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game plan was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

    Recent findings suggest that in principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

    Industry observers note that the extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

    Industry observers note that the central matter with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

    Both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

    Recent findings suggest that in general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

    Industry observers note that sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

    Recent findings suggest that towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

    According to recent reports, from there, Hoffenheim attempted to play swiftly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

    In the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

    The biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

    Recent findings suggest that there were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

    A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

    Recent findings suggest that although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

    According to recent reports, for Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing challenges ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

    Towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

    Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could quickly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

    The conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

    However, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”.

    Postecoglou’s team also showed deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

    • The goalkeeper involved in the collision that killed Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel has been seen in public for the first time since the tragic accident.
    • During a match earlier this month, Andorra keeper Jesus Owono came flying out of his goal and wiped out Tenerife star de Miguel with a high challenge which resulted in the striker being admitted to intensive care, where he later died.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER.

    Published: 06:20 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 06:30 EST, 21 November 2026.

    The goalkeeper involved in the collision that killed Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel has been seen in public for the first time since the tragic accident.

    During a match earlier this month, Andorra keeper Jesus Owono came flying out of his goal and wiped out Tenerife star de Miguel with a high challenge which resulted in the striker being admitted to intensive care, where he later died.

    De Miguel's passing shocked the footballing world and Owono was subsequently given a 12-match ban by authorities.

    Both sides have been back in action since the tragedy, but on Friday, Andorra hosted Leganes at their Estadi de la FAF.

    That was their first home game since de Miguel's passing, and they made sure to pay a moving tribute to him on the night.

    Before the match, the players went onto the pitch wearing shirts with his name and number on them and they carried out a bouquet of white flowers.

    Andorra keeper Jesus Owono was seen in public for the first time since Jesus de Miguel's tragic death as he attended a tribute to the former Tenerife star.

    Before Andorra's game with Legannes, several tributes were paid, including a minute's silence.

    A minute's silence was also held before the game, while those in attendance applauded during the ninth minute of the match, the shirt number worn by de Miguel at Tenerife.

    The most striking part of the evening though was Owono's attendance in the stands.

    The goalkeeper has stayed away from the public eye since de Miguel's death, after which he was subjected to chants of 'murderer', but he wanted to attend the tribute at his club's home ground.

    Owono was wearing a black coat and hat as he stood next to team-mates who weren't involved in the matchday squad.

    Despite receiving the support of the crowd and his team-mates, local reports stated Owono cut a downcast figure and that he was seen praying immediately after the minute's silence.

    Owono's desire to attend the tribute came after he had also asked to meet de Miguel's family, something he hopes to do one day.

    Meanwhile, Tenerife returned to action last week against AD Ceuta CF in a match that was also filled with tributes.

    Players provided a floral tribute as they arrived for the match, and gathered outside gate nine of the Heliodoro Rodríguez Lopez Stadium – another nod to de Miguel's shirt number.

    Grief-stricken Tenerife stars then took to the field carrying a bouquet of flowers, and placed it at the scene of the tragedy.

    Both sets of players and fans then observed a minute's silence in memory of de Miguel before the game kicked off.

    The game was then brought to a pause in the ninth minute, so the players could pay another tribute.

    Fans inside the stadium unveiled a tifo which read: 'Jesus de Miguel, 9, eternal blanquiazul', which translates to: 'Jesus de Miguel, 9, eternally white and blue.'.

    Recent findings suggest that other fans held up white and blue cards beside the tifo, with others in the ground applauding. When Tenerife scored, de Miguel's shirt was held in the air.

    After the game, which Tenerife won 2-0, both teams gathered in the centre circle to place de Miguel's shirt on a bouquet of flowers, and the fans applauded to bring an end to an emotional day.

    Owono was watching the game from the stands as he stood next to some of his team-mates.

    Tenerife returned to action last week and paid several tributes to their former star de Miguel.

    The tragedy occurred as the game between Tenerife and Andorra entered the seventh minute of stoppage time, when de Miguel looked set to race away on the counter-attack for his side in search of a winner.

    As he watched a long ball drop into his path, the striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line.

    After initially rolling around on the floor, de Miguel became motionless, and medical staff rushed onto the pitch to attend to him.

    Owono was given a red card for the challenge before the decision was soon taken by the referee to abandon the fixture.

    Owono's 12-match ban is currently in effect, yet his manager Carles Manso hinted that he may never play again.

    He noted: 'We will ​give him space so that he feels completely free to make ‌any ⁠decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.

    'When he feels it is appropriate and when ​he feels genuinely ready to take a ​decision ⁠like that (he will do so).'.

    #176241. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1281 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The major prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.
    • The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.
    • There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The major prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.

    The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

    Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.

    Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

    According to recent reports, since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

    The recent track record here claims this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

    Industry observers note that there isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

    He's stellar. Pretty much all the time.

    Sources indicate that also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

    There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

    We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a upcoming procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

    The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

    Recent findings suggest that skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

    Sources indicate that I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

    Recent findings suggest that again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. His nine-year deal means it'll run through his age-38 season.

    Industry observers note that for those so worried about the long-term finances of the Cohen family, are you sure you're really worried that Skubal won't be productive through five, six or even all nine years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

    In a recent development, A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

    It has been revealed that yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

    Industry observers note that gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

    Sources indicate that stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

    Recent findings suggest that justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

    Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

    According to recent reports, david Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

    According to recent reports, corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

    According to recent reports, zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

    Sources indicate that CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

    Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

    We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

    Sources indicate that by this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:.

    Are you sure a 9-year, $450 million deal for this guy is a "risk?".

    I think we could argue that it'll be a bargain.

    #176239. Breaking: Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH
